simple: Home internet was a phone call. The computer’s modem rang the internet company, beeping and screeching, and while you were online, nobody could use the phone.
technical: Dial-up: a modem at 28.8 kbit/s (56k came in 1997; V.90 in 1998) calls the ISP’s modem bank, and PPP gives the PC its own public address. No Wi‑Fi, no router, no NAT.

describe.simple: A big beige computer with a deep screen, and a keyboard on a cable. Its modem sits on a shelf, blinking, and phones the internet company.
describe.technical: A desktop PC: its external modem dials the ISP on the phone line, with no router in between.

on-the-go.simple: Out and about, hardly anyone went online, but you could: a laptop with a cable to a mobile phone rang the internet company. Three times slower than at home, and every minute cost money.
on-the-go.technical: GSM circuit-switched data: 9.6 kbit/s in one radio time slot, billed per minute like a call. The mobile switch’s modems (the IWF) call the ISP like a home modem; GPRS’s always-on packets came in 2000.

describe.simple: A thick laptop with a curly cable to a mobile phone the size of a brick, on the street.
describe.technical: A 1995 laptop with a GSM data card on a cable to a GSM phone, dialling the ISP at 9.6 kbit/s.

router.technical: Routed: longest-prefix match on the destination, TTL − 1, and a new link frame.
